newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian central bank begins operations.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian central bank begins operations.

text.p: Bosnia's new central bank formally launched operations on Monday and said it would only work through electronic transactions because political leaders are still arguing over the design of a common currency.
"For the time being, the central bank is going to work basically with electronic money," Serge Robert, the French governor of the central bank board, told a news conference.

Serb, Moslem and Croat leaders in Bosnia approved a law establishing the post-war central bank in June but they have been unable to agree on the design of an interim common currency -- a politically charged issue.

Under the country's 1995 peace treaty, the central bank operates as a currency board with full reserve backing for the new currency -- the convertible mark. The common currency is pegged one to one with the German mark.
Until an agreement is reached on the design of the convertible mark, the existing Bosnian dinar will remain in circulation, Robert said.
Banks holding the Bosnian dinar have been required to convert assets and liabilities into the new currency at a rate of 100 dinars to one convertible mark.
As of Monday, national banks in the country's Serb and Moslem-Croat territories have "ceased to act as central banks", he said.

The establishment of the central bank should attract more reconstruction aid and foreign investment and "lays the ground for a sound financial system throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina", said Robert, who chairs a governing board comprised of Moslem, Croat and Serb representatives.

Once politicians agree on the banknote design, the central bank will need about three months to begin printing the money and would also initiate a procedure for exchanging Bosnian dinars for convertible marks.
Four currencies are currently employed in the former Yugoslav republic, reflecting ethnic divisions produced by more than three years of war.
Apart from the German mark, the Yugoslav dinar is used in Serb-controlled territory, the Croatian kuna in Croat areas and the Bosnian dinar in mainly-Moslem territory.
Central bank legislation allows Serb authorities to use the Yugoslav dinar for official transactions during an indefinite transition period to be monitored by the International Monetary Fund.

Bosnian Serb nationalist leaders have proposed a banknote design featuring nationalist symbols such as double-headed eagles and Orthodox Christian monasteries which are offensive to their Moslem and Croat counterparts.

A U.S. delegation led by envoy Richard Holbrooke told the hardline Serb member of the collective presidency, Momcilo Krajisnik, last week that the international community would not tolerate nationalist or religous symbols on the currency, diplomats said.
U.S. General Jacques Klein, the newly-appointed deputy to the international High Representative to Bosnia, called on Bosnian leaders on Monday to settle the argument over currency design.
Klein told reporters that there was "keen frustration felt by the international community over the parties' continued unwillingness to complete the negotiations on the common coupon design".
